newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian police tell extortionist to call them.
newsitem.headline: Australian police tell extortionist to call them.

text.p: Australian police on Wednesday called on the extortionist who threatened to plant poisoned biscuits in supermarkets to contact them by next Monday, or they would halt their investigation.
"Police will wait until next Monday to hear directly from the extortionist," Queensland state police superintendent Ron Pickering told a news conference.
"If this does not occur, we believe we will be justified in assessing the threat to be over," Pickering said.

The extortionist had threatened to plant pesticide-laced biscuits in stores along the Australian east coast from Monday. The deadline passed and there have been no reports of poisoned biscuits or any further communication from the extortionist.
The extortionist threatened to poison biscuits made by Australia's largest biscuit maker, Arnotts, unless police involved in a 1991 murder case took a lie detector test.
The extortionist said police lied in giving evidence that resulted in Ron Thomas serving two life sentences for a double shooting murder he did not commit.

Thomas, who says he is innocent, on Tuesday issued a letter from jail calling on the extortionist to stop his bid to free him. "I want everyone to know that I had no part in these threats," Thomas said.
"Police call on the extortionist who purports to be acting in (Thomas') interests to now clearly withdraw the threats," Pickering said.
Police said John Bobak, for whom there is already a A$50,000 reward and a warrant in place in relation to the 1991 murders, remains the main suspect in the extortion threat.
Arnotts, a 70 percent-owned subsidiary of U.S. food giant Campbell Soup Co, withdrew all its products from supermarkets in Australia's eastern states of Queensland and New South Wales last Friday.
But the company would not say if it would return products to stores after next Monday if police did not hear from the extortionist.
"We will return to the market when we judge it is safe to do so," Arnotts managing director Chris Roberts told the news conference.
Arnotts said it would lose A$5.0 million (US$3.8 million) a week in sales and has stood down a few hundred casual staff.
The New South Wales and Queensland state governments have each offered a combined A$100,000 reward for the capture of the extortionist.
